results.summary: This project is a 4-bit ALU that also functions as a programmable clock divider and counter. It divides the 10 MHz clock to generate a 1 Hz counter by default, and displays the lower 8 bits of the counter on the 7-segment display while outputting them on the bidirectional pins. The inputs can override the default compare value to change the counting speed. The design is intended for testing the Tiny Tapeout infrastructure and includes basic arithmetic operations, though the documentation focuses on the counter aspect.

This project aims to create a VGA output driver for Arduino, generating a 640x480 60Hz signal. It currently outputs a random noise pattern and can be configured via SPI to display a solid colour or other patterns. The design is in an early stage, with features like character memory not yet fully implemented due to utilization constraints. It requires a VGA connector and an external microcontroller for control, and has been simulated but not yet fully tested on hardware.

This project is a clock divider that outputs multiple divided clock signals. The documentation is essentially empty, with placeholder text for how it works and how to test. It likely divides the input clock by powers of two, but the exact implementation and usage are not described. The design appears to be a simple experiment or test.

This project implements a 4-bit combinational multiplier and divider unit that supports both signed and unsigned operations. The multiplier uses a ripple carry array, while the divider uses a restoring array algorithm. It has error indicators for division overflow and divide-by-zero. The design was created in Logisim and exported to Verilog, and silicon tests confirm it works.

This is a USB FullSpeed/LowSpeed device controller implemented in SpinalHDL, designed to be controlled by a CPU over a Wishbone bus. It includes a TT2WB Wishbone bridge to fit the limited Tiny Tapeout I/O. The design supports up to 4 endpoints with 52 bytes of buffer, which may be insufficient for some USB classes. It requires external USB connector hardware and an FPGA or RP2040 for testing and demonstration.

This project is an open-source PWM peripheral with advanced features such as deadband generation and counter synchronization, aimed at power electronics applications. It contains three counters, each with two comparators and two deadband generators, configurable via a register file. The peripheral is controlled through a simple parallel interface, and can be tested with a microcontroller or manually using switches. External hardware is required to observe the PWM outputs.

This project implements a 4-point, 8-point, and 16-point FFT calculator using the radix-2 Cooley-Tukey algorithm with 4-bit fixed-point precision. It features a simple user interface with buttons for mode selection and data entry, and displays results on a 7-segment display. The design is intended for low-complexity circuits and includes bit-reversal ordering and a single butterfly unit. It requires external buttons and a way to input and read 8-bit data.

This project, titled 'Later', has no documentation beyond a title and placeholder text. It appears to drive a 7-segment display but its functionality is entirely unspecified. The design is likely incomplete or a template. There is not enough information to determine what it does or how to use it.

This is a factory test module for Tiny Tapeout 04. When input 0 is high, it outputs a counter on the output and bidirectional pins; otherwise it mirrors the inputs to the outputs. It is used to verify the chip's functionality. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected.

This project implements an 8-bit FIFO with a depth of 16, featuring First-Word Fall-Through read operation. It includes status flags such as empty, full, underflow, overflow, almost_empty, and almost_full. The FIFO allows communication between two parties with a limited channel, and can be tested by writing and reading items while checking status bits. Unit tests are available for further verification.
